# Processing with SNAP

`BurstProcessor` turns downloaded bursts into map-projected GeoTIFFs. It runs
SNAP once for every burst, or once for every pair of bursts, and skips products
that already exist.

## How a processing call works

Every `create_*` method takes the bursts, the output map projection, and
optionally a settings object. From the settings, s1bursts builds the SNAP
processing graph, the chain of SNAP steps that turns a burst into a product.
The settings describe how to process and suit every burst alike. The projection
depends on where the bursts are, so it is passed separately as `crs`:

```{.python}
from pyproj import CRS
from s1bursts import BackscatterConfig, BurstProcessor

processor = BurstProcessor(fm)
rtc = processor.create_backscatter(
    bursts, crs=CRS("EPSG:32632"), config=BackscatterConfig(grid_spacing=20),
)
```

For `crs`, the UTM zone of your study area is usually the right choice. Use the
same projection for every product you want to compare or composite. If you plan
to [composite](compositing.qmd), choose it before processing: composites accept
only products in the UTM zone and pixel size of their grid square. Without
`config`, the defaults apply, and they suit most uses.

Each product has its own method and settings object:

| Method | Input | Settings | Product |
|---|---|---|---|
| `create_backscatter()` | Bursts | `BackscatterConfig` | Backscatter of each acquisition |
| `create_coherences()` | Pairs | `CoherenceConfig` | Coherence between two acquisitions |
| `create_interferograms()` | Pairs | `InterferogramConfig` | Phase difference between two acquisitions |

The settings objects share most fields. The one you are most likely to change
is the pixel size, `grid_spacing`, which is 10 m by default; a smaller pixel
size does not add detail beyond what the radar resolves. The
[API reference](../reference/snap_graph.BackscatterConfig.qmd) lists every
setting and its default.

[SNAP processing](snap-processing.qmd) explains the steps each graph runs and
how to inspect the graph your settings produce.

## Backscatter

Backscatter describes how strongly the ground reflects the radar signal on one
date. In mountains, it also depends on the angle of each slope to the
satellite: slopes facing the satellite look bright, and slopes facing away look
dark. By default, s1bursts removes this effect with radiometric terrain
correction (RTC), following the terrain-flattening method of
[Small (2011)](https://doi.org/10.1109/TGRS.2011.2120616). RTC divides each
pixel by the area of ground that contributed to it, so the remaining
differences in brightness come from the surface itself. The result is called
gamma-0 (`gamma0`).

Use RTC unless you have a reason not to; only RTC products can be composited
with [resolution weighting](resolution-weighting.qmd). Set
`flatten_terrain=False` for geometrically terrain-corrected (GTC) backscatter,
called beta-0 (`beta0`), which places pixels correctly on the map but keeps the
slope brightness:

```{.python}
gtc = processor.create_backscatter(
    bursts, crs=crs, config=BackscatterConfig(flatten_terrain=False),
)
```

## Coherence

Coherence measures how similar two acquisitions of the same footprint are, from
0 to 1. It drops wherever the surface changed between the two dates, for
example through snowfall, melt or vegetation growth. The pairs come from
[`find_pairs()`](finding-and-downloading.qmd#pair-acquisitions):

```{.python}
pairs = bursts.find_pairs(baseline=12)
coherence = processor.create_coherences(pairs, crs=crs)
```

Coherence is estimated over a small window of neighbouring pixels, set by
`CoherenceConfig(window=...)`. A larger window gives smoother values at a
coarser resolution.

`create_interferograms()` takes the same pairs and writes the interferometric
phase. s1bursts does not unwrap that phase, so turning it into displacement
needs other software.

## Run several jobs at once

`SNAPConfig` sets how many SNAP processes run in parallel and how much memory
they share. Pass it to the processor to override the
[environment variables](environment-variables.qmd#snap):

```{.python}
from s1bursts import SNAPConfig

processor = BurstProcessor(fm, config=SNAPConfig(max_workers=2, max_ram_gb=16))
```

More processes finish a batch sooner but split the memory budget between them.
If SNAP runs out of memory, use fewer processes or a larger budget.

## Reprocessing and failures

A product whose file already exists is not processed again, so a script can be
rerun after an interruption.

::: {.callout-warning}
## Changed settings do not trigger reprocessing

Filenames describe the burst and date, not the settings. Write each experiment
to its own `FileManager` directory, or pass `overwrite=True`.
:::

A failed burst does not stop the batch by default. Each call returns an
`OperationSummary`; check its `failed_items` before using the results, since a
time series with silent gaps can mislead. Pass `continue_on_error=False` to
`BurstProcessor` to stop at the first failure instead.
